Question five. A metric went up twenty percent week over week. How do you investigate? State your assumptions, then take it apart. Is it real, or a tracking change, bot traffic, or a deploy? Which region, platform or cohort moved? Is it the day of the week, or the season? And did the denominator move? Here, conversion went from three percent to three point six: up twenty percent. But orders fell four percent. Sessions fell twenty. The rate rose because the traffic dropped. Finish with the most likely driver, and what you'd check next. Two questions about the edges of the data.

Question six. What are percentiles and quartiles? A percentile is a cut. The ninetieth percentile is the value with about ninety percent of the data at or below it. Quartiles cut at twenty-five, fifty and seventy-five. Here are thirteen amounts, in order. Q one is ten, the median twelve, Q three thirteen. Between them, the I Q R: three. The ninetieth percentile is a hundred fifty-four point eight, an amount nobody spent. Pandas interpolates between fourteen and one ninety. Other tools use other rules, so exact answers can differ. Question seven. How do you identify outliers? The I Q R rule puts a fence one and a half I Q Rs past each quartile: here, at five and a half and seventeen and a half. Two hundred and one ninety are outside. A z-score counts standard deviations from the mean. But those two drag the mean up to thirty-nine and a half, and the standard deviation to sixty-nine. So two hundred is only two point three two out. With a cutoff of two, both are caught. With three, nothing is: the outliers hide themselves. Either way, look before you delete. An outlier can be a typo, or the most important row you have. The last three are about saying it out loud.
